motivation: The paper addresses the challenge of asking clarification questions in conversational agent design. While large language models (LLMs) have shown remarkable capabilities in two-need conversations involving task-oriented clarification or retrieval-related clarification, the effectiveness of these agents in the broader range of human-computer interactions (HCI) is underexplored. Existing methods often fail to address multiple user needs simultaneously, leading to suboptimal performance in real-world HCI scenarios. This is further exacerbated by the limitations of existing benchmarks, which are often narrow in scope and fail to capture the complexities of human-computer interactions. The paper aims to bridge this gap by exploring the complexities of HCI, specifically the different user needs, interaction styles, and interaction types. It investigates two different user needs, task-oriented and retrieval-related, to understand when and why user needs are not met. The paper builds on Pearl's causality framework to propose an interaction graph framework for HCI, which includes user actions and LLM actions. This framework captures the complexities of real-world HCI interactions, facilitating exploration and analysis. The paper uses this framework to create a new benchmark, U-CAN, which addresses the limitations of existing benchmarks and provides a more comprehensive evaluation of HCI performance. The goal is to develop a more robust and effective method for asking clarification questions that can better meet user needs in real-world HCI scenarios.
idea: The paper presents U-CAN (User-Guided Clarification for Asking Across Needs), a method that leverages interaction graphs to capture the complexities of human-computer interactions, aiming to meet multiple user needs in conversations. The paper introduces a new benchmark, U-CAN, which includes 491 Enrolled Student and 352 Tutor, designed to evaluate the effectiveness of HCI methods in addressing task-oriented and retrieval-related clarification. The study finds that existing methods show performance gaps between simulated and Enrolled Student settings, highlighting the need for user-guided clarification and interaction graph designs. The paper demonstrates that HCI can be facilitated by interaction graphs and proposes an interactive graph model to further improve HCI performance.
title: U-CAN: User-Guided Clarification for Asking Clarification in Asking Across Needs Framework
abstract:
\begin{center}
    \textcolor{red}{\bingenwink}. It is still unclear if and how methods developed specifically on asking clarification for retrieval or problem-solving in the academic community can effectively address user needs during human-computer interactions (HCI).
    In this work, we first propose an \underline{\textbf{Asking Across Needs}} (\textbf{AAN}) framework to explore the complexities of HCI, including user needs, interaction styles, and interaction types, by building an interaction graph~\citep{Pearl09a} containing \textit{user} and \textit{\underline{LLM} action}s.
    Then, we create a new benchmark, \textbf{\underline{U}}s\textbf{\underline{C}}larification for \textbf{\underline{A}}sking \textbf{\underline{N}}eeds (\textbf{U-CAN}), containing \textit{task-oriented asking clarification} and \textit{retrieval-related asking clarification} which align with real-world HCI scenarios.
    Specifically, we design new interaction graph designs and user-guided prompting techniques based on our AAN framework to address multiple user needs not met in existing HCI studies.
    We find that task-oriented needs are often left unmet, and existing methods show performance gaps between simulated and real-world (enrolled students) settings.
    We also demonstrate that HCI can be facilitated by interaction graphs on retrieval-related asking clarification using our proposed interactive graph model.

Experimental_Setup.name: Preliminary Investigation
Experimental_Setup.description: The preliminary investigation aims to demonstrate the limitations of existing methods when applied to the Enrolled Student setting of the U-CAN benchmark. The study focuses on two specific datasets: the Task-oriented need dataset, which includes 10 examples, and the Retrieval-related need dataset, which includes 10 examples. These datasets are curated to understand the limitations of current methods. The experiment compares the performance of several models, including Commercial GPT-4, GPT-4 Path, CodeGen, RephraseAndRespond, and StarGate, in terms of user satisfaction, clarification, and helpfulness scores. The purpose is to highlight the challenges faced by existing methods in the Enrolled Student setting and the need for user guidance in HCI.

Experimental_Setup.name: User-Guided Prompt
Experimental_Setup.description: The User-Guided Prompt experiment investigates whether prompting techniques alone can help models meet multiple user needs in the Enrolled Student setting. The experiment compares the performance of commercial GPT-4 and M2Lingual between the existing HCI setting and the User-Guided HCI setting. The User-Guided Prompt includes two types of user guidance: user background and interaction graph. The purpose is to understand the impact of user guidance on HCI performance. The experiment involves evaluating the models' performance based on user satisfaction, clarification, and helpfulness scores.

Experimental_Setup.name: Interaction Graph Designer
Experimental_Setup.description: The Interaction Graph Designer experiment proposes two new designs: User-Guided Askable Clarification Question (U-G-ACQ) and User-Guided Actionable Response (U-G-AR). The U-G-ACQ design generates a human-written actionable clarification question (ACQ) to meet multiple user needs at the cost of an additional user-guided user action (UA). The U-G-AR design includes user-guided actionable responses in the prompting of the interaction graph designer to meet unmet user needs from the user action branch. The purpose is to bridge the gap in meeting unmet task-oriented needs. The experiment involves evaluating the models' performance based on user satisfaction, clarification, and helpfulness scores, with both human and automated metrics considered.

Experimental_Setup.name: User Action Simulator
Experimental_Setup.description: The User Action Simulator experiment focuses on retrieval-related asking clarification studies and compares commercial GPT-4's performance between the existing HCI setting and the User-Guided U-CAN setting. The purpose is to investigate whether prompting techniques alone can help models meet multiple user needs in the Enrolled Student setting. The experiment evaluates the models' performance based on user satisfaction, clarification, and helpfulness scores.

Experimental_Setup.name: Real-World Evaluation
Experimental_Setup.description: The real-world evaluation aims to demonstrate the generalizability of the U-CAN benchmark by conducting experiments in real-world settings. The experiment involves two settings: Asking Clarification in the Wild and Asking Clarification with Human Annotation. The Asking Clarification in the Wild setting uses real enrolled students and tutors in a classroom, with the models' responses evaluated by the actual enrolled students. The Asking Clarification with Human Annotation setting collects responses from models and asks real human annotators to annotate their responses, imitating the process in the U-CAN benchmark. The purpose is to validate the data quality of the U-CAN benchmark in real-world settings and provide a more comprehensive evaluation of the models' performance.
